section_summary: This section contains Japanese party declarations and policy material, followed by U.S. reports and correspondence on the occupation, political purges, labor, reparations, and industrial recovery. It also contains public opinion surveys on Japanese cabinets, political parties, constitutional questions, inflation, and daily life. The final pamphlet continues beyond page 587.

subfiles.title: Party policy proposals on finance, labor, and social policy
subfiles.about: Proposals address taxation, banking, wages, unions, welfare, housing, and repatriation.
subfiles.summary: Continuation of a party platform covering economic and social reforms.

subfiles.title: Declaration, platform, and basic policy of a new Japanese party
subfiles.about: A new party sets out its founding principles and detailed political, economic, educational, and social policies.
subfiles.summary: The declaration calls for democratic government, production, individual opportunity, and Japan’s reconstruction. The basic policy proposes electoral and administrative reform, economic liberalization, industrial recovery, tax changes, labor cooperation, welfare, and repatriation.

subfiles.title: Appeal for the formation of a new party
subfiles.about: The appeal urges formation of a progressive popular party to stabilize politics and rebuild Japan.
subfiles.summary: Calls for political unity, increased production, renewed trade, and responsible government.

subfiles.title: Party rules
subfiles.about: Rules define party officers, branches, membership, discipline, finances, and regional districts.
subfiles.summary: Articles specify selection and duties of officers, local organization, admission and expulsion, dues, donations, and amendments.

subfiles.title: Incoming airgram record sheet
subfiles.about: A State Department record sheet identifies an incoming airgram.
subfiles.summary: Records receipt and routing of a Tokyo airgram.

subfiles.title: Status of the Purges in Japan
subfiles.about: The memorandum assesses the extent, methods, and future problems of occupation purges.
subfiles.summary: It estimates that most purges are complete and about 200,000 people have been excluded from public or influential posts. It anticipates pressure to reinstate capable purgees for economic recovery while emphasizing the continuing need for democratic Japanese leadership.

subfiles.title: Incoming telegram record sheet
subfiles.about: A record sheet identifies an incoming telegram from Tokyo.
subfiles.summary: Records receipt and routing of a Tokyo telegram.

subfiles.title: Letter concerning Yoshio Osawa’s purge appeal
subfiles.about: Butterworth asks for the status and grounds of Yoshio Osawa’s purge appeal.
subfiles.summary: Butterworth cites Osawa’s American education and reputation, seeking an answer for his concerned acquaintances.

subfiles.title: Shanghai telegram proposing Woo Kyatang’s visit to Japan
subfiles.about: The consulate proposes a reporting visit to Japan by Shanghai editor Woo Kyatang.
subfiles.summary: It seeks SCAP invitational orders for Woo to write articles countering Chinese criticism of U.S. policy toward Japan.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on Woo Kyatang’s proposed visit
subfiles.about: The writer reports discussions with the Army about inviting Woo Kyatang to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Major King promises to cable Tokyo while noting budget and precedent concerns about invitational orders.

subfiles.title: Observations Made as a Result of an Orientation Visit to Kyushu
subfiles.about: Sebald forwards a Foreign Service officer’s observations from a visit to Kyushu.
subfiles.summary: The despatch summarizes Japanese concerns about labor relations, reparations, decentralization, transportation, and purges. It suggests that misunderstanding of occupation objectives calls for more effective public information and education.

subfiles.title: Observations Made as a Result of a Visit to Kyushu
subfiles.to: Office of the U.S. Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Lawrence reports interviews and site visits in four Kyushu prefectures.
subfiles.summary: Based on visits to factories, shipyards, a coal mine, and local officials, Lawrence describes disputes between labor and management and uncertainty caused by reparations and industrial decentralization. He discusses shortages, transport and coal production, and the loss of experienced personnel through purges. Interviewees repeatedly link these issues to obstacles to economic rehabilitation.

subfiles.title: List of Japanese officials and business people met during Kyushu trip
subfiles.about: The enclosure lists Japanese officials and business representatives interviewed in Kyushu.
subfiles.summary: Names and positions are listed by prefecture; much of the OCR is illegible.

subfiles.title: Corrected incoming telegram record
subfiles.about: A corrected telegram copy is logged for distribution.
subfiles.summary: Records a corrected incoming telegram and its routing.

subfiles.title: Voided incoming telegram copy
subfiles.about: An original incoming telegram is marked void in favor of the corrected copy.
subfiles.summary: Directs readers to the corrected copy.

subfiles.title: Reply approving Woo Kyatang’s proposed visit
subfiles.about: The Department approves the proposed reporting visit and hopes Woo can travel immediately.
subfiles.summary: Concurs with Shanghai’s proposal for Woo’s Japan visit.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of Japanese Public Opinion Surveys
subfiles.from: Acting U.S. Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: The despatch forwards a survey of Tokyo views on the Ashida Cabinet, parties, and Diet dissolution.
subfiles.summary: It describes the survey series, assesses the polling agency, and lists forthcoming studies.

subfiles.title: Current Japanese Public Opinion Surveys, No. 1: Attitudes of Tokyo Residents Toward the Ashida Cabinet
subfiles.from: Civil Information and Education Section, SCAP
subfiles.about: The report analyzes a February 1948 poll of Tokyo residents following Ashida’s selection as prime minister.
subfiles.summary: A sample of 516 respondents showed little enthusiasm for the Ashida Cabinet, stronger support for the Liberal Party, and plurality support for dissolving the Diet. Tables break responses down by sex and age. The report compares earlier Katayama Cabinet polls and evaluates the sample’s strengths and limits.

subfiles.title: Pamphlet Describing Results of Japanese Public Opinion Polls
subfiles.from: Acting U.S. Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: The despatch forwards a pamphlet on Japanese opinion since the war.
subfiles.summary: Transmits Yasuo Tatsuki’s survey of polling methods and political, economic, and social attitudes.

subfiles.title: General Trend of Japanese Opinion Following the End of War
subfiles.from: Yasuo Tatsuki, Japan Institute of Pacific Studies
subfiles.about: The pamphlet reviews postwar Japanese polling and public attitudes toward politics, constitutional reform, and inflation.
subfiles.summary: Tatsuki surveys polling methods and reports results on support for the Yoshida and Katayama Cabinets and political parties. He examines views on the emperor system, renunciation of war, Diet structure, and dissolution by plebiscite. The visible pages begin a section on inflation and household finances; the pamphlet continues after page 587.
